A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FraGNNet and contain readable main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The substantial revision can be reliably compared after matching relocated and renamed material.

before.justification: v1 reports original NIST20 spectrum-prediction, compound-retrieval, ablation, and annotation-consistency results in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original prediction and retrieval experiments, formula-annotation evaluation, revised ensemble analyses, and inference-speed measurements.

M1.justification: The core fragmentation procedure, two-stage neural model, and losses remain. v2 additionally evaluates ensemble predictors that average latent distributions and spectra (Appendix A.16), whereas v1 uses ensembles to compare individual-model annotations and majority agreement.

E1.justification: NIST20 spectrum prediction and PubChem-based retrieval remain within the same Orbitrap [M+H]+ domain. v2 adds formula-annotation evaluation against NIST20 expert labels (Section 5.3), also using those labels to construct the GrAFF-MS formula library. This is a bounded expansion of tasks and supervision rather than a new dataset or domain.

E2.justification: v2 adds GrAFF-MS and Precursor-Only as evaluated spectrum-prediction comparators; GrAFF-MS was previously only cited. It also reports an ICEBERG batching-bug correction and removes FraGNNet-D3 from retrieval comparisons. ICEBERG-ADV persists as ICEBERG (+OptFrag) in Table 8, so its renaming and relocation are not a new baseline.

E3.justification: Hungarian matching changes from pair-dependent 10 ppm tolerance to true-mass-dependent tolerance with a 0.002 Da floor. Retrieval expands from Hungarian cosine ranking to multiple similarities, intensity transformations, and model-specific best-ranking selections. Ablations move from validation to test data, and annotation experiments change from two D3 ensemble configurations to four D4 configurations.

E4.justification: The annotation analysis changes from within-ensemble consensus and majority voting to individual-versus-ensemble predictions and agreement across four entropy configurations. v2 adds retrieval-ranking sensitivity analyses, DAG precision statistics, and runtime benchmarking. Collision-energy and edge ablations remain, but the D4 (+Edges) result in v1 Table 6 is absent from v2 Table 7.

E5.justification: Five-seed means and standard deviations already accompany prediction and ablation results in v1. v2 extends this reporting to retrieval, where v1 provided point estimates, and adds individual-model standard-deviation bars to ensemble plots. This establishes expanded uncertainty reporting, not an increase in runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces D4 InChIKey cosine scores of 0.717/0.691 with 0.736/0.709, while main-table retrieval Top-1 changes from 23.8% to 36.0%. Changed matching and retrieval protocols prevent treating these uniformly as same-setting gains. New formula-annotation results report F1 scores of 0.89 for D4, 0.74 for GrAFF-MS, and 0.79 for ICEBERG; ensemble and runtime findings are also added.

T1.justification: v2 tightens Definition 4.1 to single-edge-removal transitions and corrects the recall formula's normalization. It adds a short entropy-concavity proof for ensembling, a derivation relating Jensen-Shannon and spectral-entropy similarity, and revised annotation-agreement definitions. The central probabilistic formulation and loss mathematics remain.

C1.justification: The central probabilistic-fragmentation contribution and state-of-the-art prediction/retrieval claims remain. The contribution list replaces scalability with prediction error as an explicitly advertised property, and the discussion extends its stated practical-utility claim to peak annotation.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes using annotation disagreement to flag unreliable explanations; v2 emphasizes robust ensemble-mode agreement despite entropy differences, while retaining the distinction between consistency and chemical correctness. v2 also adds explanations for weak edge-ablation effects and qualifications concerning fragment-merging self-edges and implementation-dependent runtime comparisons.

D1.justification: v2 adds detailed preprocessing filters, fragment-merging implementation information, baseline training details, a code-access link, a 100-trial hyperparameter-search description, and timing hardware and batching settings. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing that every newly described setting changed. Conversely, most exact software-version pins from v1 Appendix L are removed.

R1.justification: v2 updates the literature with works including MassSpecGym, DiffMS, FIORA, and MadGen, and adds annotation and entropy-metric references. It sharpens the distinction between FraGNNet's latent distributions and ICEBERG's binned outputs. The existing binned/structured taxonomy and much of the CFM/ICEBERG positioning already present in v1 Appendix C remain.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the background and annotation narrative, clarifies formula versus fragment annotations, and replaces resolution terminology with mass accuracy throughout. It reorganizes baseline discussions and appendices, separates formula evaluation from fragment consistency, and adds author-contribution and acknowledgement sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, and major tables are redesigned to place dataset splits side by side. Out-of-support results move to a separate appendix table. Ensemble bar charts and agreement heatmaps replace the earlier annotation tables, additional evaluation tables appear, and existing illustrative figures are visually revised.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the paper's interpretability and practical-utility claims through expert-label formula evaluation, broader baseline comparisons, retrieval uncertainty reporting, and runtime measurements. Expanded preprocessing and implementation documentation also makes the work more assessable and reproducible. Although exact dependency versions are lost and changed protocols prevent simple cross-version performance claims, these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.
